catalog_quote: Unlike the metrical system of a language like English, where there is a clear rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables, Tommo So’s metrical structure is rather vaporous. However, certain phonological rules suggest a stem-initial strong-weak trochee [σ́σ̆]. This trochaic pattern does not continue throughout longer words – there is no sense of undulating rhythm as in a typical stress language. There is only evidence for this single foot, which comes from the following: 1. Vowel reduction to a high vowel or schwa in σ2 position [(C)VCV] 2. new_statements.rule_in_words: Tommo So is a tone language (H, L, extensive grammatical tone overlays) with no audible rhythmic stress; the only metrical structure the author finds is a single left-aligned (stem-initial) trochee: the first syllable of the stem is strong and the second syllable is weak (it undergoes vowel reduction to a high vowel/schwa, post-sonorant syncope in verbs, and /g/ lenition), 'particularly in longer words' (p. 9, p. 66-67: 'no weakening is ever found in syllables other than the second syllable'). If coded positionally this is stem-initial prominence, but the author explicitly declines to call it a stress system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'This trochaic pattern does not continue throughout longer words – there is no sense of undulating rhythm'; only one foot per stem. (The 2010 draft, sec. 3.2.3, notes that long words/crypto-compounds behave as compounds, 'generally but not always split into two trochees [σ́σ̆-σ́σ̆]', i.e. each compound member has its own initial trochee.)
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllabic words may have a long vowel in the second syllable, so the weak-σ2 restriction is operative mainly in longer words (p. 43 snippet); post-sonorant syncope applies only in verbs and verbal nouns and only to the 2nd syllable of CVCV stems before coronal-stop suffixes (p. 67); a few /LHL/ trisyllabic nouns are Fulfulde loans whose tone pattern reflects Fulfulde stress (p. 86 snippet).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem (stem-initial trochee), not the phonological word or phrase; evidence is segmental (reduction/syncope/lenition), not pitch or perceived prominence; tone is lexical/grammatical and independent of this foot.
new_statements.identity_note: McPherson's description is based mainly on the Tédié (Tédjé) commune variety of Tommo So on the Bandiagara-Douentza plateau (grammar p. 9 names Tédié speakers); language-level glottocode tomm1242, no separate dialect code needed. The 2010 draft spells the language 'Tɔmmɔ-Sɔ'.

Tommo So shows the effects of a single left-aligned trochee, in that the second syllable, particularly in longer words, tends to be metrically weak.' p. 86 (snippet): a handful of /LHL/ nouns are Fulfulde loans whose tone mimics Fulfulde stress. sources.note: Sec. 3.2.2 'Metrical structure' (pp. 15-16): same statement in earlier wording: 'Unlike the metrical system in a language like English.. Tɔmmɔ-Sɔ's meter is rather vaporous. That being said, certain phonological rules suggest an underlying metrical structure, with a stem-initial strong-weak trochee [σ́σ̆]. This trochaic pattern does not continue throughout longer words—there is no sense of undulating rhythm as in a typical stress language. There is but one initial trochee.' Sec. 3.2.3 adds that crypto-compounds are 'generally but not always split into two trochees [σ́σ̆-σ́σ̆]'.
